family_history: Father: PKD with cerebral aneurysm (ruptured at age 52)

patient.chief_complaint: Sudden severe headache this morning while at work, brief loss of consciousness
patient.history_present_illness: Ms. Rodriguez is a 50-year-old woman with polycystic kidney disease and a strong family history of cerebral aneurysm who presents after sudden onset of the worst headache of her life at work this morning. She was at her desk when she experienced an instantaneous explosion of severe headache, 10/10, immediately followed by brief loss of consciousness lasting approximately 30-60 seconds. Coworkers witnessed her slump in her chair and called 911. By EMS arrival, she was awake but confused. On transport, she vomited twice. In the ED, she is now alert and fully oriented. She reports persistent headache 8/10 with neck stiffness. She has had intermittent headaches in the past, but nothing of this severity or character. She specifically notes she was placed on a surveillance MRA program 3 years ago after her father died from a ruptured aneurysm (PKD-associated), and her last MRA 18 months ago showed no aneurysm. She was due for repeat imaging in 6 months. She is extremely anxious about her diagnosis. She denies ongoing focal weakness, visual changes, or speech difficulty. PKD was diagnosed 12 years ago; her renal function has been stable.

output.summary: PKD patients have 4-5x increased risk of intracranial aneurysm (prevalence 9-12%). MRA surveillance recommended for PKD patients with family history of SAH or aneurysm. This patient had a surveillance program but aneurysm developed between screening intervals - risk of interval aneurysm formation/growth. First-degree relatives with PKD should also be screened.

key_reasoning_points: PKD is associated with a 4-5x increased risk of intracranial aneurysm; family history further compounds this risk
This patient had surveillance but the aneurysm developed between 18-month intervals, illustrating interval rupture risk in PKD
Hyponatremia in SAH must be distinguished between cerebral salt wasting (CSW, hypovolemic - treat with saline) and SIADH (euvolemic - treat with fluid restriction)
High urine sodium (>40 mEq/L) with volume depletion signs indicates CSW, not SIADH
QTc 524 ms with hypokalemia creates critical arrhythmia risk - Torsades de Pointes
